{{Short description|Statement in complex analysis}}
In [[complex analysis]], a branch of [[mathematics]], the '''Koebe 1/4 theorem''' states the following:

<blockquote>'''Koebe Quarter Theorem.''' The image of an injective analytic function <math>f:\mathbf{D}\to\mathbb{C}</math> from the [[unit disk]] 
<math>\mathbf{D}</math> onto a [[subset]] of the [[complex plane]] contains the disk whose center is <math>f(0)</math> and whose radius is <math>|f'(0)|/4</math>.</blockquote>

The theorem is named after [[Paul Koebe]], who conjectured the result in 1907. The theorem was proven by [[Ludwig Bieberbach]] in 1916. The example of the [[#Koebe_function|Koebe function]] shows that the constant <math>1/4</math> in the theorem cannot be improved (increased).

A related result is the [[Schwarz lemma]], and a notion related to both is [[conformal radius]].

==Grönwall's area theorem<!--'Gronwall's area theorem' redirects here-->==
{{Main|Area theorem (conformal mapping)}}
Suppose that 

:<math>g(z) = z +b_1z^{-1} + b_2 z^{-2} + \cdots</math>

is univalent in <math>|z|>1</math>. Then

:<math>\sum_{n=1}^\infty n|b_n|^2 \le 1.</math>

In fact, if <math>r > 1</math>, the complement of the image of the disk <math>|z|>r</math> is a bounded domain <math>X(r)</math>. Its area is given by

:<math> \int_{X(r)} dx\,dy = {1\over 2i} \int_{\partial X(r)}\overline{z}\,dz = {1\over 2i}\int_{|z|=r}\overline{g}\,dg=\pi r^2 - \pi\sum_{n=1}^\infty n|b_n|^2 r^{-2n}.</math>

Since the area is positive, the result follows by letting <math>r</math> decrease to <math>1</math>. The above proof shows equality holds if and only if the complement of the image of <math>g</math> has zero area, i.e. [[Lebesgue measure]] zero.

This result was proved in 1914 by the Swedish mathematician [[Thomas Hakon Grönwall]].

==Koebe function<!--'Koebe function' redirects here-->==
The '''Koebe function''' is defined by 

:<math>f(z)=\frac{z}{(1 - z)^2}=\sum_{n=1}^\infty n z^n</math>

Application of the theorem to this function shows that the constant <math>1/4</math> in the theorem cannot be improved, as the image domain 
<math>f(\mathbf{D})</math> does not contain the point <math>z=-1/4</math> and so cannot contain any disk centred at <math>0</math> with radius larger than <math>1/4</math>.

The '''rotated Koebe function''' is 

:<math>f_\alpha(z)=\frac{z}{(1-\alpha z)^2}=\sum_{n=1}^\infty n\alpha^{n-1} z^n</math>

with <math>\alpha</math> a [[complex number]] of [[absolute value]] <math>1</math>. The Koebe function and its rotations are ''[[Schlicht function|schlicht]]'': that is, [[Univalent function|univalent]] (analytic and [[Injective function|one-to-one]]) and satisfying <math>f(0)=0</math> and <math>f'(0)=1</math>.

==Bieberbach's coefficient inequality for univalent functions<!--'Bieberbach's inequality' redirects here-->==
Let

:<math> g(z) = z + a_2z^2 + a_3 z^3 + \cdots </math>

be univalent in <math>|z|<1</math>.  Then

:<math>|a_2|\le 2.</math>

This follows by applying Gronwall's area theorem to the odd univalent function 

:<math> g(z^{-2})^{-1/2}= z -{1\over 2} a_2 z^{-1} + \cdots. </math>

Equality holds if and only if <math>g</math> is a rotated Koebe function.

This result was proved by [[Ludwig Bieberbach]] in 1916 and provided the basis for his [[Bieberbach conjecture|celebrated conjecture]] that 
<math>|a_n|\leq n</math>, proved in 1985 by [[Louis de Branges]].

==Proof of quarter theorem==
Applying an affine map, it can be assumed that 

:<math>f(0)=0,\,\,\, f^\prime(0)=1,</math>

so that 

:<math> f(z) = z + a_2 z^2 + \cdots .</math>

In particular, the coefficient inequality gives that <math>|a_2| \le 2</math>.
If <math>w</math> is not in <math>f(\mathbf{D})</math>, then

:<math>h(z)={wf(z)\over w-f(z)} = z +(a_2+w^{-1}) z^2 + \cdots </math>

is univalent in <math>|z|<1</math>.

Applying the coefficient inequality to <math>h</math> gives

:<math> |w|^{-1} = |w^{-1}| = |-a_2 + a_2 + w^{-1}| \le |a_2| + |a_2 + w^{-1}|\le 4, </math>

so that 

:<math> |w|\ge {1\over 4}.</math>

==Koebe distortion theorem==
The '''Koebe distortion theorem''' gives a series of bounds for a univalent function and its derivative. It is a direct consequence of Bieberbach's inequality for the second coefficient and the Koebe quarter theorem.<ref>{{harvnb|Pommerenke|1975|pp=21–22}}</ref> 

Let <math>f(z)</math> be a univalent function on <math>|z|<1</math> normalized so that <math>f(0)=0</math> and <math>f'(0)=1</math> and let <math>r=|z|</math>. Then

:<math>{r \over (1+r)^2}\le |f(z)|\le {r\over (1-r)^2}</math>

:<math>{1-r\over (1+r)^3} \le |f^\prime(z)| \le {1+r\over (1-r)^3}</math>

:<math>{1-r\over 1+r} \le \left|z{f^\prime(z)\over f(z)}\right| \le {1+r\over 1-r}</math>

with equality if and only if <math>f</math> is a Koebe function 

:<math> f(z) ={z\over(1-e^{i\theta}z)^2}. </math>
